terms: Roman Britain
Britain as a Roman province from AD 43 (Claudian invasion) until c. AD 410, leaving roads, towns and Christianity.
Anglo-Saxons
Germanic peoples (Angles, Saxons, Jutes) who settled Britain after c. 450, forming kingdoms such as Wessex and Mercia.
Witan
Anglo-Saxon council of nobles and clergy that advised the king and could confirm royal succession.
Norman Conquest
William of Normandy's invasion of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.
Feudalism
Hierarchical landholding system in which the king granted fiefs to tenants-in-chief in return for military service.
Domesday Book
1086 survey of land and resources commissioned by William I to assess tax and consolidate Norman rule.
First Crusade
Expedition launched after Urban II's 1095 sermon at Clermont, capturing Jerusalem in July 1099.
Crusader States
Latin polities founded in the Levant after 1099, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem and County of Tripoli.
Saladin
Sultan of Egypt and Syria who recaptured Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.
Third Crusade
1189-92 campaign led by Richard I, Philip II and Frederick Barbarossa, securing a truce with Saladin.
Papal Monarchy
Twelfth- and thirteenth-century papacy claiming supreme authority over Christendom, exemplified by Innocent III.
Indulgence
Remission of temporal punishment for sin, granted by the Church to crusaders and later sold widely.
Tenant-in-chief
Noble holding land directly from the king in return for knight service and counsel.
Manorialism
Economic system in which peasants worked a lord's demesne in exchange for protection and use of strips.
Villein
Unfree peasant tied to the manor, owing labour services and unable to leave without the lord's permission.
Common Law
Body of judge-made law developed under Henry II from the 1160s, applied across the realm.
Magna Carta
Charter sealed by King John at Runnymede on 15 June 1215 limiting royal power and protecting baronial rights.
Clause 39
Magna Carta provision that no free man should be imprisoned or dispossessed except by lawful judgement of peers or the law of the land.
Dawes Plan 1924
American Charles Dawes restructured reparations; US loans fuelled brief Weimar 'Golden Age'.
Kapp Putsch 1920
Right-wing coup by Wolfgang Kapp and Freikorps; defeated by general strike, exposed army's hostility to Republic.
Night of the Long Knives 1934
30 June purge: Hitler's SS murdered SA leader Ernst Rohm and around 200 others, securing army support.
Ruhr Crisis 1923
French-Belgian occupation after reparations default; passive resistance caused hyperinflation and political collapse.
Spartacist Uprising 1919
Communist revolt in Berlin led by Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg; crushed by Freikorps with government approval.
Wannsee Conference 1942
20 January meeting led by Heydrich coordinating 'Final Solution'; bureaucratic plan for extermination of European Jews.
Coup of Brumaire 1799
Napoleon Bonaparte's seizure of power in November 1799 that overthrew the Directory and established the Consulate, ending the revolutionary republic.
Declaration of the Rights of Man 1789
Foundational text of August 1789 proclaiming liberty, equality and popular sovereignty, dismantling the privileges of the old regime.
Estates-General 1789
Assembly of three estates summoned by Louis XVI to address France's fiscal crisis, last met in 1614, sparking the revolution when the Third Estate broke away.
Storming of the Bastille 1789
On 14 July 1789 a Paris crowd seized the royal fortress-prison, a symbol of monarchical tyranny, marking the popular outbreak of the revolution.
The Terror 1793-94
Period of mass executions directed by Robespierre's Committee of Public Safety against suspected enemies of the revolution, ending with his fall.
Thermidorian Reaction 1794
The overthrow and execution of Robespierre in July 1794, ending the Terror and ushering in the more moderate Directory regime.
Battle of Bosworth 1485
Henry Tudor defeated Richard III ending Wars of the Roses; legitimised through marriage to Elizabeth of York 1486.
Break with Rome 1533-34
Act of Appeals (1533) and Act of Supremacy (1534) severed papal authority over English Church for Henry's annulment.
Council Learned in the Law
Henry VII's body using bonds and recognisances to control nobility; Empson and Dudley made it notorious.
Elizabethan Settlement 1559
Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity creating moderate Protestant Church; Royal Injunctions enforced Book of Common Prayer.
Mid-Tudor Crisis 1547-58
Period of instability: Edward VI's Protestant reforms, Mary I's Catholic restoration, succession disputes, Wyatt's rebellion.
Monopolies Crisis 1601
Parliament protested at Elizabeth's grants of trade monopolies; Golden Speech promised reform but issue passed to Stuarts.
Execution of Charles I 1649
30 January beheading at Whitehall after Rump Parliament trial; first regicide of an anointed European king.
Glorious Revolution 1688
William of Orange invited to replace James II; Bill of Rights (1689) established constitutional monarchy.
Gunpowder Plot 1605
Catholic conspiracy led by Robert Catesby; Guy Fawkes caught beneath Lords with 36 barrels of gunpowder.
Petition of Right 1628
Parliament's statement against Charles I's forced loans, arbitrary imprisonment and martial law; Charles dissolved parliament 1629.
Restoration 1660
Charles II returned after Cromwell's death and Monck's march; Declaration of Breda promised religious toleration.
Ship Money
Charles I's tax on coastal counties extended inland 1635; Hampden's 1637 legal challenge mobilised opposition.

terms: Battle of Hattin 1187
Saladin's decisive victory destroying the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, leading directly to his recapture of Jerusalem and the Third Crusade.
Battle of Manzikert 1071
Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantine army and captured Emperor Romanos IV, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement and prompting later appeals to the West.
Capture of Jerusalem 1099
The First Crusade's bloody conquest of the holy city from its Muslim rulers, establishing Latin Christian control after a successful siege.
Council of Clermont 1095
Pope Urban II's sermon calling Western knights to aid Byzantium and recover Jerusalem, launching the First Crusade with the cry 'God wills it'.
Sack of Constantinople 1204
The Fourth Crusade, diverted from Egypt, captured and looted the Christian Byzantine capital, fatally weakening the empire it had set out to aid.
The Crusader States
Latin principalities founded in the East after 1099, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem and County of Edessa, collectively called Outremer.
GI Bill 1944
Servicemen's Readjustment Act provided returning veterans with college tuition, mortgages and unemployment pay; created suburban middle class.
Great Society 1964-65
Johnson's reforms: Medicare, Medicaid, Voting Rights Act, immigration reform, War on Poverty.
McCarthyism
Senator Joseph McCarthy's 1950-54 anti-communist witch hunts; HUAC investigations, Hollywood blacklist, fall of State Department officials.
Roe v Wade 1973
Supreme Court 7-2 ruling that constitutional right to privacy covered abortion; landmark of second-wave feminism.
Stonewall 1969
28 June police raid on Greenwich Village gay bar sparked riots; catalyst for gay liberation movement.
Watergate 1972-74
Nixon's cover-up of DNC headquarters break-in; impeachment proceedings forced resignation on 9 August 1974.
Big Bang 1986
Thatcher's deregulation of London Stock Exchange; abolished fixed commissions, allowed foreign ownership, transformed City.
Butskellism
Post-war consensus combining Conservative Butler and Labour Gaitskell; mixed economy, full employment, welfare state.
Falklands War 1982
Argentina invaded 2 April; British task force retook islands by 14 June; Thatcher's popularity rescued.
Suez Crisis 1956
Eden's collusion with France and Israel to seize canal from Nasser; US pressure forced humiliating withdrawal, ended Eden's career.
Three-Day Week 1974
Heath's response to NUM miners' strike and oil crisis; electricity restricted, prompted February election loss.
Winter of Discontent 1978-79
Public sector strikes under Callaghan; rubbish uncollected, dead unburied; led to Thatcher's victory May 1979.

Détente
Period of reduced superpower tension c.1969-79, associated with Nixon-Kissinger and Brezhnev: SALT I, Helsinki Accords.
SALT I 1972
Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty signed 26 May 1972, capping ICBMs and SLBMs and including the ABM Treaty.
Helsinki Accords 1975
Final Act of the CSCE: recognition of post-war borders alongside human-rights commitments (Basket III).
Soviet-Afghan War
Soviet intervention from December 1979 to February 1989; helped end détente and drained Soviet resources.
Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI)
Reagan's 1983 'Star Wars' missile defence proposal, pressuring Soviet military spending.
Perestroika and Glasnost
Gorbachev's 1985-91 policies of economic restructuring and political openness that loosened the Soviet system.
Korean War 1950-53
Conflict triggered by North Korean invasion on 25 June 1950; UN/US forces under MacArthur fought DPRK and Chinese troops; armistice 27 July 1953.
NSC-68
April 1950 US policy paper urging massive defence build-up against the Soviet threat, adopted after Korea began.
Hungarian Rising 1956
Nationalist uprising under Imre Nagy crushed by Soviet invasion 4 November 1956; ~2,500 Hungarians killed.
Berlin Wall 1961
Barrier begun on 13 August 1961 to stem East German emigration via West Berlin; symbol of the divided continent.
Cuban Missile Crisis
13-day standoff (16-28 October 1962) over Soviet medium-range missiles in Cuba, resolved by withdrawal and secret US pledge to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)
Strategic doctrine that nuclear war would destroy both superpowers, deterring first use.
Yalta Conference
4-11 February 1945 meeting of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill agreeing UN creation, German occupation zones and 'free elections' in Eastern Europe.
Potsdam Conference
17 July-2 August 1945 meeting of Stalin, Truman and Churchill/Attlee; revealed widening Allied disagreement over Eastern Europe and reparations.
Long Telegram and X Article
George Kennan's 1946 cable and 1947 'Sources of Soviet Conduct' article advocating containment of Soviet expansion.
Truman Doctrine 1947
12 March 1947 address pledging US support to peoples 'resisting attempted subjugation', triggered by Greek and Turkish crises.
Marshall Plan
European Recovery Programme (June 1947 proposal, 1948 act) providing ~$13 billion in aid to Western Europe.
NATO 1949
North Atlantic Treaty Organisation founded on 4 April 1949 by 12 states; Article 5 mutual defence pledge.
February Revolution 1917
Petrograd uprising in early March (Old Style February) that forced Nicholas II's abdication on 15 March 1917.
Dual Power
March-November 1917 coexistence of the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, weakening both.
April Theses
Lenin's programme on return from exile (April 1917): 'Peace, Land, Bread' and 'All Power to the Soviets'.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik seizure of Petrograd on 25 October (Old Style) / 7 November (New Style) 1917 by the Military Revolutionary Committee.
War Communism
1918-21 emergency policies: grain requisitioning (prodrazvyorstka), nationalisation, labour conscription.
New Economic Policy 1921
Lenin's tactical retreat permitting small-scale private trade and a tax in kind, introduced at the Tenth Party Congress.
Five-Year Plans
Centrally directed industrial plans from October 1928 prioritising heavy industry; First Plan 1928-32.
Collectivisation
1929-33 forced amalgamation of peasant farms into kolkhozes and sovkhozes, accompanied by 'dekulakisation' and the Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) of 1932-33.
Great Terror 1936-38
Mass purges including the Moscow Show Trials, the Yezhovshchina, and the Order 00447 operation; up to ~700,000 executed.
Great Patriotic War
Soviet term for the 1941-45 conflict beginning with Operation Barbarossa on 22 June 1941; approximately 27 million Soviet dead.
Secret Speech 1956
Khrushchev's address to the Twentieth Party Congress on 25 February 1956 denouncing Stalin's cult of personality.
Virgin Lands Scheme
Khrushchev's 1954 programme to cultivate Kazakh and Siberian steppe; initially successful, later dogged by soil exhaustion.
Emancipation Edict 1861
Alexander II's decree freeing approximately 23 million serfs, requiring redemption payments and creating the village mir.
Zemstva
Elected local councils introduced in 1864 to administer rural welfare, education and roads.
Russification
Alexander III and Nicholas II's policy of imposing Russian language, religion and culture on national minorities.
Bloody Sunday 1905
Massacre of peaceful petitioners led by Father Gapon outside the Winter Palace on 22 January 1905.
October Manifesto 1905
Nicholas II's promise of civil liberties and an elected Duma, ending the general strike and splitting the opposition.
Stolypin's Agrarian Reforms
From 1906, dismantling the mir to create independent peasant farmers ('wager on the strong'); coupled with field-court repression.
Battle of Bosworth 1485
Henry Tudor's defeat of Richard III on 22 August 1485, founding the Tudor dynasty.
Star Chamber
Royal court under Henry VII used to enforce law against over-mighty subjects and curb retaining.
Bonds and Recognisances
Financial sureties imposed by Henry VII to bind nobles to good behaviour and tighten royal control.
Act in Restraint of Appeals 1533
Statute drafted by Thomas Cromwell declaring England 'an empire' free from papal jurisdiction, enabling Henry's divorce.
Act of Supremacy 1534
Statute declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England, completing the legal break with Rome.
Dissolution of the Monasteries
1536-40 closure of religious houses under Cromwell, transferring vast lands and wealth to the Crown.
Somerset's Protectorate
Edward Seymour's rule 1547-49 as Lord Protector for Edward VI, ended by political failure and the 1549 rebellions.
First Book of Common Prayer 1549
Cranmer's liturgy, moderately Protestant, imposed by the Act of Uniformity 1549; triggered the Prayer Book Rebellion.
Second Book of Common Prayer 1552
Sharply Protestant revision rejecting the real presence; symbol of Edward's reformation.
Lady Jane Grey
Protestant claimant proclaimed queen for nine days in July 1553 by Northumberland; executed 1554.
Marian Restoration
Mary I's 1553-58 reversal of Edwardian reform: restoring the Mass, papal authority (Pole's reconciliation 1554) and burning ~283 Protestants.
Loss of Calais 1558
Final English continental possession lost to France in January 1558, a blow to Marian prestige.
Elizabethan Settlement 1559
Acts of Supremacy (Elizabeth as Supreme Governor) and Uniformity establishing a moderate Protestant national church.
Act of Uniformity 1559
Statute reimposing the Book of Common Prayer (a hybrid of 1549/1552) and mandating attendance under penalty.
Thirty-Nine Articles 1563
Doctrinal statement of the Church of England, finalised in 1571, defining its Protestant theology.
Mary Queen of Scots
Catholic heir presumptive imprisoned in England 1568-87; executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587 after the Babington Plot.
Babington Plot 1586
Catholic conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth and free Mary, exposed by Walsingham's intelligence network.
Spanish Armada 1588
Fleet of 130 ships sent by Philip II in summer 1588, defeated in the Channel (Gravelines, 8 August) and wrecked off Scotland and Ireland.
Reconstruction 1865-77
Post-Civil War effort to readmit Southern states and protect freedpeople; ended by the Compromise of 1877.
Thirteenth, Fourteenth, Fifteenth Amendments
Reconstruction Amendments (1865, 1868, 1870) abolishing slavery, granting birthright citizenship and equal protection, and prohibiting racial barriers to the vote.
Jim Crow
System of state-level segregation laws emerging in the South from the 1880s, validated by Plessy v Ferguson 1896.
Gilded Age
Term coined by Mark Twain for c.1870-1900: rapid industrialisation, immigration, urbanisation, political corruption.
Sherman Antitrust Act 1890
First federal statute against trusts and monopolies, weakly enforced until Theodore Roosevelt's 'trust-busting'.
Progressive Era
c.1890-1920 reform movement targeting corporate power, corruption and social ills; key figures Theodore Roosevelt, Wilson; muckrakers like Sinclair.
Roaring Twenties
1920s era of consumer prosperity, mass culture, jazz, automobile growth and stock speculation, alongside Prohibition and immigration restriction.
Wall Street Crash 1929
Stock market collapse 24-29 October 1929 (Black Thursday/Tuesday) wiping out around 25% of market value in days.
Great Depression
Economic catastrophe 1929-c.1939: unemployment peaked at ~25% (1933); 9,000 banks failed by 1933.
Hundred Days 1933
FDR's opening session of Congress (9 March-16 June 1933) passing 15 major laws including the Emergency Banking Act and AAA.
Alphabet Agencies
New Deal programmes such as CCC, TVA, WPA, NRA, SSA providing relief, recovery and reform.
Social Security Act 1935
Second New Deal law establishing federal old-age pensions, unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children.
Pearl Harbor
Japanese attack on the US Pacific Fleet at Hawaii on 7 December 1941, bringing the US into the Second World War.
Brown v Board of Education 1954
Supreme Court ruling that 'separate but equal' public schooling was unconstitutional, overturning Plessy.
Civil Rights Act 1964
Lyndon Johnson's law outlawing racial discrimination in employment and public accommodations.
Voting Rights Act 1965
Federal statute banning literacy tests and authorising federal oversight of voter registration in the South.
Gulf of Tonkin Resolution 1964
Congressional authorisation for President Johnson to use military force in Vietnam following alleged North Vietnamese attacks.
Watergate
Political scandal arising from the 17 June 1972 break-in at the DNC office; led to Nixon's resignation on 9 August 1974.
Battle of Plassey 1757
Robert Clive's victory over Siraj-ud-Daulah of Bengal, securing East India Company dominance in Bengal and marking the start of territorial empire.
East India Company (EIC)
Chartered English trading company (1600) that acquired diwani rights in 1765 and governed vast Indian territories until 1858.
Diwani of Bengal 1765
Right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted by Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, giving the Company fiscal sovereignty.
Doctrine of Lapse
Annexation policy under Dalhousie (1848-56) absorbing princely states without natural male heirs, fuelling resentment.
1857 Rebellion
Major uprising sparked by sepoy grievances (greased cartridges) that spread across northern India and prompted the abolition of Company rule.
Government of India Act 1858
Statute transferring EIC powers to the Crown, creating the Secretary of State for India and ending Company government.
Satyagraha
Gandhi's doctrine of 'truth-force' non-violent civil disobedience, first developed in South Africa and applied in India from 1917.
Salt March 1930
240-mile march to Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly, launching the Civil Disobedience movement.
Government of India Act 1935
Major statute granting provincial autonomy and envisaging an all-India federation; basis of Congress ministries 1937.
Quit India 1942
Mass movement launched by Congress on 8 August 1942 demanding immediate British withdrawal; leaders were imprisoned.
Mountbatten Plan
Last Viceroy's 3 June 1947 plan to partition British India into India and Pakistan, with independence on 15 August 1947.
Partition 1947
Division of British India along the Radcliffe Line, causing mass migration of an estimated 10-15 million people and up to 1 million deaths in communal violence.
The Raj
Direct British Crown rule in India from 1858 to 1947, administered by a Viceroy and the Indian Civil Service.
Indian Civil Service (ICS)
Elite administrative cadre, overwhelmingly British until late nineteenth century, governing districts and provinces.
Indian National Congress (INC)
Political organisation founded in Bombay in December 1885, initially moderate and loyalist, later spearheading the independence movement.
Partition of Bengal 1905
Curzon's administrative division of Bengal, widely seen as divide-and-rule, sparking the Swadeshi movement; reversed in 1911.
Rowlatt Act 1919
Legislation extending wartime detention powers, provoking nationwide protest led by Gandhi.
Amritsar Massacre 1919
Jallianwala Bagh shooting on 13 April 1919 when General Dyer's troops killed several hundred unarmed Indians, a turning point against the Raj.

Henry Tudor's defeat and killing of Richard III, ending the Wars of the Roses and founding the Tudor dynasty as Henry VII.

Henry VIII's closure of religious houses, seizing their wealth and land to fund the crown and reward loyal nobles and gentry.
Mid-Tudor Crisis 1547-58
Period of religious upheaval, rebellion and instability under Edward VI and Mary I, testing the strength of crown and government.
Star Chamber
A royal prerogative court strengthened under the early Tudors to enforce order over overmighty subjects and bypass the slower common-law courts.
The Reformation Parliament 1529-36
Sessions of Parliament that passed Henry VIII's break with Rome, establishing royal supremacy over the Church of England.
Wars of the Roses 1455-87
Dynastic civil wars between the houses of Lancaster and York for the English crown, weakening the nobility and paving the way for Tudor rule.

Anglo-Irish Treaty 1921
Negotiated by Collins and Griffith; created Irish Free State as dominion with oath to crown; sparked civil war.
Easter Rising 1916
24-29 April Dublin rebellion led by Pearse and Connolly; crushed by British, 15 leaders executed including Connolly tied to chair.
Government of Ireland Act 1920
Partition created Northern Ireland (six counties) and Southern Ireland; established devolved Stormont parliament.
Irish Civil War 1922-23
Pro-Treaty Free State forces under Collins defeated anti-Treaty IRA led by de Valera; Collins killed August 1922.
Republic of Ireland 1949
Declared by Costello government on Easter Monday; left Commonwealth, ended remaining ties with British Crown.
Sinn Fein 1918 Landslide
Won 73 of 105 Irish seats; refused Westminster, established Dail Eireann in Dublin January 1919.
1905 Revolution
Uprising triggered by Bloody Sunday massacre; forced Tsar Nicholas II to issue October Manifesto promising Duma.
February Revolution 1917
Strikes and mutinies in Petrograd forced Nicholas II to abdicate; Provisional Government took power.
Five-Year Plans
Stalin's industrialisation programme from 1928; rapid heavy industry growth at huge human cost in gulags.
NEP 1921
New Economic Policy under Lenin allowing small private trade and ending grain requisitioning; restored agricultural output.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd led by Lenin and Trotsky; stormed Winter Palace, overthrew Provisional Government.
War Communism

Johnson's law banning discrimination in employment and public accommodations on grounds of race, sex, religion.

March on Washington 1963

Unanimous Supreme Court ruling on 17 May 1954 declaring school segregation unconstitutional.
Emmett Till
14-year-old murdered in Mississippi in August 1955; open-casket funeral galvanised national outrage.
Rosa Parks
NAACP activist whose arrest on 1 December 1955 sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
Montgomery Bus Boycott
381-day boycott (5 December 1955 - 20 December 1956) ending segregated seating after Browder v Gayle.
SCLC
Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in January 1957 by MLK to coordinate ministerial non-violence.
Little Rock Nine
Nine students escorted into Central High School in September 1957 after Eisenhower deployed 101st Airborne.
Greensboro Sit-in
Began on 1 February 1960 when four North Carolina A&T students sat at a segregated Woolworth's counter.
SNCC
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, founded April 1960 at Shaw University, advised by Ella Baker.
Freedom Rides
1961 CORE-organised journeys testing Boynton v Virginia ruling against interstate bus segregation.
James Meredith
Air Force veteran whose enrolment at Ole Miss on 1 October 1962 required federal marshals after riots.
Birmingham Campaign
SCLC campaign April-May 1963 led by MLK and Shuttlesworth; Bull Connor's tactics shocked national opinion.
Letter from Birmingham Jail
King's open letter of 16 April 1963 defending non-violent direct action and criticising white moderates.
March on Washington
28 August 1963 demonstration of 250,000 demanding jobs and freedom; site of King's 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Civil Rights Act 1964
Signed by Lyndon B. Johnson on 2 July 1964 outlawing discrimination in employment and public accommodations.
Freedom Summer
1964 SNCC-led campaign in Mississippi registering Black voters; three workers (Chaney, Goodman, Schwerner) murdered.
Selma to Montgomery
March on 7 March 1965 ('Bloody Sunday') attacked by state troopers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge.
Voting Rights Act 1965
Signed 6 August 1965 outlawing literacy tests and authorising federal registrars in covered jurisdictions.
MLK Assassination
Martin Luther King Jr. shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on 4 April 1968 by James Earl Ray.

Easing of US-Soviet tensions c. 1969-79 marked by arms control, summits and economic exchange.
SALT I
Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty signed by Nixon and Brezhnev on 26 May 1972 capping ICBMs and SLBMs.
Helsinki Accords
1 August 1975 agreement recognising borders and committing signatories to human rights.
Second Cold War
Renewed tension c. 1979-85 after Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and Reagan's military build-up.
Glasnost and Perestroika
Gorbachev's reforms of openness and restructuring from 1985 attempting to revive the Soviet economy.
Fall of the Berlin Wall
Mass crossings on 9 November 1989 after East German politburo confusion over travel rules.
Berlin Wall
Concrete barrier begun on 13 August 1961 sealing East from West Berlin until 9 November 1989.
Cuban Missile Crisis
Thirteen-day stand-off in October 1962 over Soviet missiles in Cuba, resolved by Kennedy-Khrushchev deal.
Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
1964 US congressional authorisation for war in Vietnam following alleged North Vietnamese attacks.
Tet Offensive
Coordinated Viet Cong and PAVN attacks on 30 January 1968, undermining US confidence in the war.
Vietnamization
Nixon's policy from 1969 of transferring combat duties to South Vietnamese forces while withdrawing US troops.
Paris Peace Accords
27 January 1973 agreement ending direct US combat; Saigon fell to the North on 30 April 1975.
Yalta Conference
February 1945 meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreeing on occupation zones and the UN.
Potsdam Conference
July-August 1945 conference with Truman, Stalin and Attlee finalising occupation and reparations.
Truman Doctrine
Truman's speech of 12 March 1947 committing US support to free peoples resisting subjugation.
Marshall Plan
European Recovery Programme launched in 1948 disbursing about USD 13 billion in aid by 1952.
Berlin Blockade
Soviet closure of land routes to West Berlin from 24 June 1948; broken by an airlift of 2.3 million tonnes.
NATO
North Atlantic Treaty Organisation formed on 4 April 1949 by twelve western states.
Industrial Revolution
Transformation c. 1750-1900 from agrarian to industrial economy, powered by coal, steam and factory production.
Enclosure
Conversion of common land into privately held fields, accelerating after 1760 via parliamentary Acts.
Spinning Jenny
Multi-spindle machine invented by James Hargreaves c. 1764, revolutionising cotton production.
Urbanisation
Mass migration to cities; Manchester grew from c. 25,000 in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1851.
Great Reform Act
1832 statute extending the franchise to middle-class men and redistributing seats.
Chartism
Working-class movement 1838-58 demanding the Six Points of the People's Charter, including universal male suffrage.
James II
Catholic king (1685-88) whose policies of religious toleration and standing army alarmed Anglicans.
Declaration of Indulgence
Suspension of penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters issued by James II in 1687 and 1688.
Immortal Seven
Group of Whigs and Tories who invited William of Orange to invade in June 1688.
Glorious Revolution
1688-89 deposition of James II and joint accession of William III and Mary II.
Bill of Rights
1689 statute establishing parliamentary supremacy, prohibiting Catholic monarchs and free elections.

1701 Act vesting succession in the Protestant House of Hanover after Anne.
Personal Rule
Charles I's eleven-year rule without Parliament, 1629-40, funded by ship money and prerogative income.
Long Parliament
Parliament summoned in November 1640 that impeached Strafford and passed reforms before war.
New Model Army
Professional parliamentary army created in 1645 under Fairfax and Cromwell.
Battle of Naseby
Decisive parliamentary victory on 14 June 1645 destroying Charles I's main field army.
Pride's Purge
Forcible exclusion of moderate MPs by Colonel Pride on 6 December 1648, creating the Rump Parliament.
Regicide
Trial and execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649 outside the Banqueting House.
English Civil War 1642-49
Armed conflict between Royalists supporting the king and Parliamentarians, ending in defeat for Charles I and the rise of the New Model Army.
Execution of Charles I 1649
The trial and beheading of Charles I for treason against his people, an unprecedented act establishing a republican Commonwealth.
Long Parliament 1640
Parliament summoned by Charles I to fund war with Scotland, which instead attacked royal policies, escalating tensions toward civil war.
Personal Rule 1629-40
The eleven years Charles I governed without Parliament, raising revenue by controversial means like Ship Money, deepening conflict with his subjects.
The Glorious Revolution 1688
The overthrow of James II and accession of William and Mary, leading to the Bill of Rights and a constitutional limit on royal power.
The Restoration 1660
The return of the monarchy under Charles II after the collapse of the republic, restoring king, Lords and the Church of England.

Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government in Petrograd, establishing the first communist state in Russia.
Russian Civil War 1918-21
Conflict between the Bolshevik Reds and anti-Bolshevik Whites, won by the Reds, consolidating communist control across the former empire.

War in South Africa revealing weaknesses in British tactics and the poor health of recruits, spurring further army reform.

President Hoover's belief in limited government intervention, blamed for failing to relieve Depression suffering and his 1932 election defeat.

The severe economic slump of the 1930s bringing mass unemployment, bank failures and poverty across the United States.

The 1920s economic boom in the USA marked by mass production, consumer credit, rising share prices and cultural change before the crash.

The sudden collapse of US stock prices in October 1929, wiping out fortunes and triggering the worldwide Great Depression.
Wartime Recovery 1941-45
The boost to US industry and employment from Second World War production, which finally ended the Depression and revived the economy.

1945 Labour Government

National Health Service
Established by Bevan's 1946 Act; opened on 5 July 1948, providing care free at the point of use.
British Nationality Act 1948
Granted CUKC status to Commonwealth citizens; underpinned the SS Empire Windrush (22 June 1948) and post-war immigration.
Post-war Consensus
Bipartisan acceptance of full employment, the mixed economy, the welfare state and conciliation of trade unions, c.1945-79.
Winter of Discontent 1978-79
Wave of public-sector strikes against Labour's 5% pay policy, contributing to Callaghan's defeat in May 1979.
Representation of the People Act 1918
Extended the franchise to all men aged 21+ and to women over 30 meeting a property qualification.
Equal Franchise Act 1928
Lowered women's voting age to 21, achieving universal adult suffrage on equal terms.
General Strike 1926
Nine-day TUC sympathy strike (3-12 May 1926) in support of locked-out miners; collapsed without concessions.
Great Depression in Britain
1929-c.1933 slump: unemployment peaked at 22% (1932); industrial regions (Jarrow, South Wales) hardest hit.
National Government 1931
Cross-party coalition under Ramsay MacDonald formed 24 August 1931 in response to the financial crisis.
Jarrow Crusade
200-strong march from Jarrow to London (5-31 October 1936) protesting unemployment in the North East.
Compromise of 1850
Series of laws including a stronger Fugitive Slave Act, admitting California free and creating Utah/New Mexico territories on popular sovereignty.
Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854
Stephen Douglas's law repealing the Missouri Compromise and triggering 'Bleeding Kansas'.
Dred Scott decision 1857
Supreme Court ruling that African Americans were not citizens and Congress could not bar slavery from territories.
Emancipation Proclamation 1863
Lincoln's executive order of 1 January 1863 freeing enslaved people in Confederate-held areas.
Reconstruction Amendments
13th (1865), 14th (1868) and 15th (1870) Amendments abolishing slavery, guaranteeing citizenship/equal protection and prohibiting racial barriers to voting.
Compromise of 1877
Informal deal awarding the disputed 1876 presidency to Hayes in return for the withdrawal of federal troops from the South.
Plessy v Ferguson 1896
Supreme Court ruling sustaining 'separate but equal' Louisiana railway segregation, legitimising Jim Crow.
Booker T Washington
Educator (1856-1915), founder of Tuskegee Institute (1881); 'Atlanta Compromise' speech (1895) advocating accommodation.
W. E. B. Du Bois
Scholar and activist (1868-1963) who critiqued Washington in The Souls of Black Folk (1903) and demanded political rights.
NAACP
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People founded on 12 February 1909, pursuing legal challenges to segregation.
Great Migration
Movement of about 6 million African Americans from the rural South to Northern and Western cities 1910-70.
Harlem Renaissance
1920s cultural flowering of African American literature, music and art centred on Harlem, New York.
Brown v Board of Education 1954
Unanimous Supreme Court ruling on 17 May 1954 that segregated public schools violated the 14th Amendment.
Montgomery Bus Boycott
1 December 1955-20 December 1956 protest after Rosa Parks's arrest; ended in desegregation of buses (Browder v Gayle).
Civil Rights Act 1964
Federal law signed 2 July 1964 banning discrimination in employment and public accommodations.
Voting Rights Act 1965
Signed 6 August 1965; banned literacy tests and authorised federal supervision of registration.
Black Power
Movement from 1966 emphasising self-determination, associated with Stokely Carmichael, SNCC and the Black Panthers (1966).
Barack Obama
Elected 4 November 2008 as the first African American president of the United States; inaugurated 20 January 2009.
People's Republic of China
Proclaimed by Mao Zedong from Tiananmen Gate on 1 October 1949 after CCP victory in the civil war.
Common Programme 1949
Interim constitution adopted by the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference; basis of New Democracy.
Sino-Soviet Treaty 1950
Treaty of Friendship signed 14 February 1950 with Stalin, providing Soviet loans, advisers and a security alliance.
Korean War 1950-53
PRC sent the People's Volunteer Army across the Yalu in October 1950; Armistice 27 July 1953.
Land Reform 1950-52
Mass redistribution of land; 'speak bitterness' sessions; perhaps 1-2 million landlords killed.
First Five-Year Plan 1953-57
Soviet-style heavy industry drive doubling steel output; basis of the 1954 PRC Constitution.
Cultural Revolution
Mao's 1966-76 mass campaign against 'capitalist roaders' and the 'Four Olds', mobilising youth and persecuting officials and intellectuals.
Little Red Book
Quotations from Chairman Mao compiled by Lin Biao from 1964; printed in billions of copies.
Red Guards
Student paramilitary groups (from 1966) attacking teachers, officials and traditional culture.
Down to the Countryside
Rustication of about 17 million urban youth (1968-78) to learn from peasants and ease urban turmoil.
Lin Biao Affair 1971
Designated successor Lin Biao allegedly plotted against Mao and died in an air crash in Mongolia on 13 September 1971.
Gang of Four
Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen; radical leaders arrested on 6 October 1976 after Mao's death.
Hundred Flowers Campaign 1956-57
Mao's invitation to 'let a hundred flowers bloom' encouraging criticism; followed by the Anti-Rightist crackdown from June 1957.
Anti-Rightist Campaign
Purge from 1957 in which an estimated 550,000 intellectuals were labelled rightists and persecuted.
Great Leap Forward 1958-62
Mao's drive for rapid industrialisation and full collectivisation via People's Communes.
People's Communes
Large rural units of about 5,000 households introduced from August 1958, organising labour, food and welfare communally.
Backyard Furnaces
Small village steel furnaces producing poor-quality 'pig iron'; symbol of misallocated effort in 1958-59.
Great Chinese Famine
1959-62 famine following the Leap; demographic studies suggest around 30 million excess deaths.
Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
Peace signed 3 March 1918 ceding Poland, the Baltics, Ukraine and Finland to the Central Powers.
War Communism
1918-21 emergency policy: grain requisitioning, nationalisation, labour conscription, ration cards.
Cheka
Secret police founded December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky, instrument of the Red Terror.
Kronstadt Mutiny 1921
Sailors' uprising at Kronstadt naval base (28 February-18 March 1921) demanding 'Soviets without Bolsheviks'.
New Economic Policy 1921
Introduced at the Tenth Party Congress: tax in kind replaced requisitioning; small-scale private trade legalised.
Lenin's Testament

Rasputin
Siberian mystic influential at court; murdered on 30 December 1916 by conservative aristocrats.
February Revolution 1917

Provisional Government
Liberal-led cabinet March-November 1917, headed by Lvov then Kerensky from July.
Petrograd Soviet
Workers' and soldiers' council formed 12 March 1917; Order No. 1 placed military authority under Soviet control.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik insurrection on 25 October (OS) / 7 November (NS) 1917, organised by the Military Revolutionary Committee.
Nicholas II
Last Tsar of Russia 1894-1917, committed to autocracy; abdicated on 15 March 1917 (New Style).

Nicholas II's promise of civil rights and an elected Duma, drafted by Witte to defuse the general strike.

Constitution issued 23 April 1906 reserving autocratic prerogatives and undermining the Duma.
Pyotr Stolypin
Prime Minister 1906-11 combining harsh repression ('Stolypin necktie') with agrarian reforms; assassinated September 1911.
Wind of Change
Macmillan's speech to the South African Parliament on 3 February 1960 acknowledging African nationalism.
Ghana
First sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence, on 6 March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah.
Mau Mau
Kenyan insurgency 1952-60 against British settler rule; declared state of emergency October 1952.
Algerian War
1954-62 French colonial war ending in Algerian independence and the fall of France's Fourth Republic.
Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
1953-63 British settler federation dissolved amid African nationalist pressure.
UDI
Ian Smith's Unilateral Declaration of Independence by Rhodesia on 11 November 1965.
Indian National Congress
Founded 1885; under Gandhi from 1920 it led mass civil disobedience for independence.
Salt March
Gandhi's 1930 protest march to Dandi against the British salt monopoly, mobilising mass non-cooperation.
Quit India
1942 Congress campaign demanding immediate British withdrawal; suppressed by mass arrests.
Partition
1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan; up to 14 million displaced and an estimated million killed.
Suez Crisis
October-November 1956 conflict after Nasser nationalised the canal; Anglo-French-Israeli action halted by US pressure.
Nasser
Egyptian president (1956-70) who nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956.
British Raj
Direct Crown rule of India from 1858, following the Government of India Act after the 1857 Rebellion.
Scramble for Africa
Partition of the continent by European powers c. 1881-1914, formalised at the Berlin Conference 1884-85.
Dominion
Self-governing settler colony; Canada (1867), Australia (1901), New Zealand (1907) and South Africa (1910).
Indirect Rule
System used in Northern Nigeria by Lugard whereby British administrators worked through local chiefs.
White Man's Burden
Kipling's 1899 phrase encapsulating imperial paternalism and civilising mission rhetoric.
Boer War
1899-1902 conflict with Afrikaner republics ending in Treaty of Vereeniging and British annexation.
Marxist History
Tradition explaining historical change through class struggle and modes of production, prominent after 1917.
E.P. Thompson
British Marxist historian whose Making of the English Working Class (1963) recovered workers' 'agency'.
Annales School
Founded by Bloch and Febvre in 1929; emphasised long-run structures, mentalites and total history.
Longue Durée
Braudel's concept of slow-moving geographic and structural change, articulated in his 1949 Mediterranean.
History from Below
Approach focusing on the experience of ordinary people, championed by Thompson and Hill.
Microhistory
Detailed study of small cases (Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms, 1976) to illuminate wider mentalities.
E.H. Carr
British historian whose 1961 lectures What is History? argued historians and facts are mutually shaping.
Geoffrey Elton
Tudor historian whose The Practice of History (1967) defended empirical method against Carr.
Hayden White
Theorist whose Metahistory (1973) argued historical writing is structured by literary tropes.
Linguistic Turn
Shift from the 1970s emphasising that historical understanding is shaped by language and discourse.
Postcolonial History
Approach problematising Eurocentric narratives; key works by Said (Orientalism 1978) and Chakrabarty.
Public History
History produced for and with public audiences in museums, broadcasting and heritage; expanding from the 1970s.
Herodotus
Fifth-century BC Greek historian whose Histories investigated the Greco-Persian Wars; called the 'father of history'.
Thucydides
Athenian historian (c. 460-400 BC) of the Peloponnesian War, emphasising eyewitness evidence and political analysis.
Annales
Roman senatorial historian Tacitus (c. AD 56-120); also French Annales School later (founded 1929).
Whig History
Tradition presenting the past as progress toward liberty and constitutional government, critiqued by Herbert Butterfield in 1931.
Leopold von Ranke
German historian (1795-1886) demanding source criticism and writing 'as it actually happened' (wie es eigentlich gewesen).
Historicism
Approach treating each era on its own terms, seeking to understand context rather than judging by present standards.
Night of the Long Knives
Purge on 30 June 1934 eliminating SA leadership including Rohm and conservative critics like Schleicher.
Fuhrer Oath
Personal oath of loyalty sworn by the armed forces to Hitler on 2 August 1934 after Hindenburg's death.
Schutzstaffel (SS)
Elite paramilitary under Himmler from 1929; expanded after 1934 to dominate police and concentration camps.
Gestapo
Secret state police created 1933 (in Prussia) and consolidated under Heydrich, central to Nazi terror.
Polycratic State
Concept used by historians like Hans Mommsen describing competing Nazi agencies under Hitler's arbitration.
Strength Through Joy
Kraft durch Freude, leisure programme of the DAF providing cheap holidays and the Volkswagen scheme.
April Boycott
One-day SA-led boycott of Jewish shops on 1 April 1933, ineffective but signalling state-sponsored persecution.
Civil Service Law
Law of 7 April 1933 dismissing Jews and political opponents from public employment.
Nuremberg Laws
Passed on 15 September 1935 stripping Jews of citizenship and prohibiting intermarriage.
Aryanisation
Forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses and property to non-Jewish Germans, accelerating after 1937.
Kristallnacht
Pogrom on 9-10 November 1938 destroying 267 synagogues, killing about 91 Jews and arresting 30,000 men.
Volksgemeinschaft
'National community' idealised as racially pure, excluding Jews, Roma and others deemed undesirable.
Hitler's Chancellorship
Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany by President Hindenburg on 30 January 1933.
Reichstag Fire
Fire on 27 February 1933 blamed on Marinus van der Lubbe and used to justify emergency decree.
Reichstag Fire Decree
Issued 28 February 1933 suspending civil liberties under Article 48.
Enabling Act
Law of 23 March 1933 (Gesetz zur Behebung der Not) granting Hitler power to legislate without parliament.
Gleichschaltung
'Coordination' of German society, abolishing trade unions on 2 May and other parties by July 1933.
Concordat
Agreement of 20 July 1933 between the Vatican and Nazi Germany guaranteeing Catholic rights in return for political withdrawal.

Under the boy-king Edward VI, England moved decisively toward Protestantism through new prayer books and the Act of Uniformity.
Elizabethan Religious Settlement 1559
Elizabeth I's compromise establishing a Protestant Church of England with the monarch as Supreme Governor, seeking to unite her divided realm.
Essex Rebellion 1601
The Earl of Essex's failed revolt against Elizabeth's court, ending in his execution and exposing tensions late in her reign.
Marian Restoration 1553-58
Mary I's attempt to restore Catholicism, including the burning of Protestant heretics, earning her the later nickname 'Bloody Mary'.
Poor Law 1601
Elizabethan legislation making parishes responsible for relieving the poor, codifying earlier measures into a national system.
Spanish Armada 1588
Philip II's failed naval invasion of England, defeated by the English fleet and storms, boosting Elizabeth's prestige and Protestant confidence.
Abyssinian War 1935-36
Mussolini's successful invasion of Ethiopia, avenging Adowa and defying the League of Nations, boosting Fascist prestige at home.
Battle of Adowa 1896
Ethiopia's crushing defeat of an invading Italian army, a humiliation that ended Italy's first attempt to colonise Abyssinia.
Giolittian Era
The period of liberal reform and political management under Giovanni Giolitti before 1914, marked by industrial growth and electoral expansion.
Italy in the First World War
Italy joined the Allies in 1915 hoping for territory, but heavy losses and disappointment at the peace fed post-war discontent.
March on Rome 1922
Mussolini's Fascist demonstration that pressured King Victor Emmanuel III into appointing him Prime Minister, beginning Fascist rule.

The consolidation of one-party Fascist control after 1925, suppressing opposition and building a totalitarian state under Il Duce.
Chinese Communist Revolution 1949
Mao Zedong's communist victory over the Nationalists, establishing the People's Republic of China and alarming the United States.

Korean War 1950-53

Nixon Visits China 1972
President Nixon's groundbreaking visit easing US-Chinese hostility, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split to reshape Cold War diplomacy.

The growing rift between communist China and the Soviet Union from the late 1950s, dividing the communist world and reshaping Cold War alignments.

The long conflict in which the USA backed South Vietnam against communist North Vietnam and the Viet Cong, ending in US withdrawal and communist victory.

Stalin and Bukharin's doctrine (1924-25) of building socialism in the USSR alone, rejecting Trotsky's permanent revolution.
Five-Year Plans
Centrally directed industrial plans from October 1928 prioritising heavy industry, steel and coal.
Collectivisation

Holodomor 1932-33
Ukrainian famine resulting from grain procurement and policy; approximately 3.5-5 million Ukrainian deaths.
Great Terror 1936-38

Non-aggression treaty signed 23 August 1939 (Molotov-Ribbentrop), with secret protocol partitioning Eastern Europe.
Operation Barbarossa
Nazi invasion of the USSR launched 22 June 1941 with 3.5 million Axis troops along an 1,800-mile front.
Union of the Crowns 1603
Accession of James VI of Scotland to the English throne on 24 March 1603, joining the two crowns under a single monarch.

Catholic conspiracy by Robert Catesby and others, including Guy Fawkes, to blow up Parliament on 5 November 1605; foiled the night before.

Doctrine, articulated by James I (e.g., The True Law of Free Monarchies), that monarchs derive authority from God alone.
Petition of Right 1628
Parliamentary statute extracted from Charles I forbidding non-parliamentary taxation, arbitrary imprisonment and billeting.
Personal Rule 1629-40
Charles I's 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' governing without Parliament; raised funds through Ship Money and prerogative levies.
Bishops' Wars 1639-40
Two Anglo-Scottish wars triggered by Charles's attempt to impose a new prayer book on Scotland (1637); forced recall of Parliament.
Test Act 1673
Required office-holders to receive Anglican communion and renounce transubstantiation; aimed at Catholics.
Exclusion Crisis 1679-81
Whig attempts to bar Charles II's Catholic brother James from the throne, defeated by Charles's dissolution of Parliament.
Glorious Revolution 1688
William of Orange's invasion (5 November 1688) leading to James II's flight and the joint accession of William III and Mary II in February 1689.
Bill of Rights 1689
Statute (December 1689) limiting royal power, requiring parliamentary consent for taxation and a standing army, and protecting parliamentary speech.
Act of Settlement 1701
Statute securing the Protestant succession via Sophia of Hanover and her heirs.
Acts of Union 1707
Joined the Parliaments of England and Scotland into the Parliament of Great Britain, effective 1 May 1707.
English Civil War 1642-49
Conflict between Royalists (Cavaliers) and Parliamentarians (Roundheads) in three phases: 1642-46, 1648 (Second), 1649 settlement.
New Model Army 1645
Reorganised Parliamentarian force created by the Self-Denying Ordinance and the February 1645 Act; led to victory at Naseby (June 1645).
Pride's Purge
Colonel Pride's 6 December 1648 exclusion of MPs unwilling to try the King, producing the Rump Parliament.
Execution of Charles I
Charles I beheaded outside the Banqueting House, Whitehall, on 30 January 1649; monarchy and Lords abolished.
Cromwell's Protectorate
Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector 1653-58 under the Instrument of Government; succeeded briefly by his son Richard.
Restoration 1660
Return of Charles II following the Declaration of Breda (4 April 1660); entered London 29 May 1660.
Battle of Bosworth 1485
22 August 1485 victory of Henry Tudor over Richard III, beginning Tudor rule.
Council Learned in the Law
Henry VII's prerogative tribunal (notably under Empson and Dudley) enforcing royal financial rights.
Treaty of Medina del Campo 1489
Alliance with Spain securing the Aragon-Tudor match; Catherine of Aragon married Arthur in 1501, then Henry VIII in 1509.
Act in Restraint of Appeals 1533
Statute drafted by Cromwell declaring England 'an empire' free from papal jurisdiction; enabled the Boleyn marriage.
Royal Supremacy
Established by the Act of Supremacy 1534 making Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Pilgrimage of Grace 1536
Major northern rising led by Robert Aske protesting the dissolution; suppressed by 1537 with the execution of about 216 rebels.
Protectorate of Somerset
Edward Seymour governed for the young Edward VI 1547-49, falling after the 1549 rebellions.
Prayer Book Rebellion 1549
West Country rising against the new English liturgy; suppressed by Lord Russell after 4,000 deaths.
Kett's Rebellion 1549
Norfolk agrarian rising under Robert Kett, defeated at Dussindale; 3,000 rebels killed.
Northumberland's Rule
John Dudley dominated 1550-53, deepening Protestant reform with the 1552 Prayer Book and Forty-Two Articles (1553).
Wyatt's Rebellion 1554
January-February Kent rising against Mary's Spanish marriage; defeated outside London.
Marian Persecution
Burning of about 283 Protestants 1555-58, immortalised in Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563).
Elizabethan Settlement 1559
Acts of Supremacy (Elizabeth as Supreme Governor) and Uniformity (1559 Prayer Book) defining the Church of England.
Puritans
Reformed Protestants seeking further reform; campaigns include the Vestments Controversy (1566) and Admonition to the Parliament (1572).
Regnans in Excelsis 1570
Papal bull excommunicating Elizabeth and absolving subjects of allegiance, sharpening recusant penalties.
Mary Queen of Scots
Catholic claimant imprisoned in England 1568-87; executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587 after the Babington Plot.
Walsingham's Spy Network
Intelligence apparatus uncovering Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586) plots.
Spanish Armada 1588
Fleet of 130 ships defeated in the Channel; broken at Gravelines on 8 August 1588 and scattered by storms.
Malleus Maleficarum
1487 inquisitorial manual by Kramer (and Sprenger) codifying witch-hunting procedure; widely reprinted by Protestants and Catholics.
Demonology
Theological doctrine of demons and witches as Satan's agents; central to early modern witch-belief.
Diabolic Pact
Allegation that witches signed a personal covenant with Satan, distinguishing learned demonology from popular maleficium.
Maleficium
Harmful magic causing illness, crop failure or death, the popular core of witch accusations.
Reformation Anxiety
Confessional uncertainty and apocalyptic expectation after Luther (1517) intensifying fears of the devil's activity.
Daemonologie 1597
Treatise by James VI of Scotland defending witch belief and the use of judicial torture; reissued in England in 1603.
Royal Society 1660
Chartered London body promoting natural philosophy; symbolised the mechanical worldview challenging diabolic agency.
Mechanical Philosophy
Cartesian-Newtonian conception of nature as law-governed matter, leaving little room for witches' supernatural action.
Balthasar Bekker
Dutch Calvinist minister whose De Betoverde Weereld (1691-93) argued the devil had no power on earth, condemned by his church.
Jane Wenham 1712
Hertfordshire woman convicted of witchcraft in March 1712 but pardoned by Queen Anne; last English conviction.
Witchcraft Act 1735
British statute (9 Geo II c. 5) repealing earlier witchcraft laws and instead criminalising the pretence of supernatural powers.
Janet Horne 1727
Old woman executed at Dornoch in Sutherland in 1727, traditionally the last person executed for witchcraft in Britain.
Matthew Hopkins
Essex 'Witchfinder General' active 1645-47, responsible for c.100 of the c.300 English executions for witchcraft.
Witch's Mark
Anomalous bodily mark seen as evidence of demonic suckling; sought through 'pricking' and 'watching'.
Manningtree Trials 1645
Hopkins's first major investigation in Essex; resulted in around 19 executions at Chelmsford in July 1645.
Salem Witch Trials 1692
Massachusetts outbreak: about 200 accused, 19 hanged, one pressed to death (Giles Corey), four died in jail.
Spectral Evidence
Testimony that the accused's spirit had appeared to torment victims; admitted at Salem and later discredited.
Court of Oyer and Terminer
Special tribunal convened by Governor Phips in May 1692 to try the Salem accused; dissolved October 1692.
People's Republic of China
Proclaimed by Mao Zedong on 1 October 1949 in Beijing after Communist victory over the Nationalists.
Land Reform
1950-53 redistribution of land from landlords to peasants, accompanied by struggle sessions and mass killings.
Hundred Flowers Campaign
1956-57 invitation to criticise the party, swiftly reversed in the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign.
Great Leap Forward
1958-62 push for collectivised communes and backyard steel; famine killed an estimated 30-45 million.
Cultural Revolution
1966-76 campaign mobilising Red Guards to attack the Four Olds and remove Mao's rivals.
Sino-Soviet Split
Breakdown of relations between Moscow and Beijing from 1960 over ideology, leadership and de-Stalinisation.
Five-Year Plan
Centrally planned industrial targets; the First Plan ran 1928-32 prioritising heavy industry.
Collectivisation
Forced merger of peasant farms into kolkhozes from 1929, eliminating kulaks as a class.
Holodomor
Famine of 1932-33 in Ukraine and Kazakhstan killing an estimated 5-7 million amid grain seizures.
Stakhanovite Movement
1935 campaign celebrating shock-workers exceeding output targets, named after miner Alexei Stakhanov.
Great Terror
Purges of 1936-38 including show trials and mass executions; about 750,000 shot under NKVD Order 00447.
Gulag
Network of labour camps administered by the NKVD; population peaked at about 2.5 million in the early 1950s.
October Revolution
Bolshevik seizure of Petrograd on 25 October 1917 (Julian; 7 November Gregorian) led by Lenin and Trotsky.
Decree on Land
First Bolshevik decree of 26 October 1917 abolishing private property in land in favour of peasant control.
Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
Punitive peace with Germany signed on 3 March 1918, ceding the Baltics, Ukraine and a quarter of Russia's population.
War Communism
1918-21 policies of grain requisitioning, nationalisation and labour militarisation to sustain the Civil War.
Cheka
Bolshevik secret police created on 20 December 1917 under Dzerzhinsky; conducted the Red Terror.
NEP
New Economic Policy from March 1921 reintroducing limited private trade and a tax in kind on peasants.
April Theses
Lenin's programme issued on his return on 3 April 1917 (OS) demanding 'all power to the Soviets' and ending the war.
Kerensky Offensive
June 1917 offensive in Galicia that collapsed and discredited the Provisional Government.
July Days
Spontaneous demonstrations in Petrograd 3-7 July 1917; Bolsheviks blamed and Lenin fled to Finland.
Kornilov Affair
August 1917 attempted coup by General Kornilov; defeat enabled Bolshevik resurgence and rearming of Red Guards.
Dual Power
Coexistence of Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet sharing legitimacy March-October 1917.
Constituent Assembly
Promised democratic body elected November 1917 but dissolved by Lenin on 6 January 1918.
Military Revolutionary Committee
Bolshevik body led by Trotsky from 9 October coordinating the seizure of power in Petrograd.
Storming the Winter Palace
Bolshevik occupation of Provisional Government headquarters on the night of 25-26 October 1917 (OS).
Sovnarkom
Council of People's Commissars established on 26 October 1917 with Lenin as chairman.
Decree on Peace
Issued 26 October 1917 calling for immediate armistice without annexations.
Decree on Land
Abolished private landownership and sanctioned peasant seizures, adopting Socialist Revolutionary policy.
Constituent Assembly Dissolution
Lenin closed the elected Assembly on 6 January 1918 after Bolsheviks won only 24 per cent of seats.
Nicholas II
Last Tsar of Russia (1894-1917), whose autocracy was discredited by military defeat and economic crisis.
Petrograd
Renamed capital (1914); centre of revolutionary events with about 2.4 million inhabitants by 1917.
International Women's Day
23 February (Old Style) / 8 March (New Style) 1917; demonstrations launched the February Revolution.
Petrograd Soviet
Council of workers' and soldiers' deputies established 27 February 1917 from earlier 1905 precedent.
Provisional Government
Liberal cabinet under Prince Lvov from 2 March 1917 sharing power with the Petrograd Soviet (dual power).
Abdication
Nicholas II abdicated for himself and his son on 2 March 1917 (OS) at Pskov.
Grain Procurement Crisis
1927 shortfall when peasants withheld grain, prompting Stalin's break with NEP.
Dekulakisation
Campaign from December 1929 deporting 'kulaks' to labour camps; about 1.8 million deported by 1932.
Kolkhoz
Collective farm pooling land, machinery and labour, paying members in proportion to work.
Sovkhoz
State farm where peasants worked as wage labourers under direct state management.
Gosplan
State Planning Commission that set Five-Year Plan targets and allocated resources.
Magnitogorsk
Steel city built from 1929 east of the Urals, embodying socialist construction and forced labour.
Kirov Assassination
Murder of Leningrad party boss Sergei Kirov on 1 December 1934, pretext for purges.
Moscow Show Trials
Public trials in 1936, 1937 and 1938 of Old Bolsheviks including Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin.
Yezhovshchina
Mass operations under NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov 1937-38; from Order 00447 of July 1937.
Order 00447
NKVD order of 30 July 1937 setting regional execution and camp quotas, targeting 'former kulaks' and criminals.
Red Army Purge
1937-38 elimination of three of five marshals and around 30,000 officers, weakening the military before 1941.
Gulag Archipelago
Soviet labour camp system named in Solzhenitsyn's 1973 work; population peaked at about 2.5 million in early 1950s.
Great Patriotic War
Soviet term for the war against Nazi Germany, 22 June 1941 to 9 May 1945, costing about 27 million Soviet lives.
Order 227
Stalin's 'Not One Step Back' order of 28 July 1942 introducing penal battalions and blocking detachments.
Stalingrad
Battle from August 1942 ending 2 February 1943 with surrender of Paulus's Sixth Army.
Yalta and Potsdam
Conferences (February and July-August 1945) shaping postwar Europe and Soviet sphere.
Zhdanovshchina
Postwar cultural campaign 1946-48 under Andrei Zhdanov enforcing socialist realism and anti-cosmopolitanism.
Doctors' Plot
Antisemitic conspiracy fabricated in January 1953 accusing Jewish doctors of plotting against Soviet leaders.
Elizabethan Settlement
1559 Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity establishing a Protestant Church of England with Elizabeth as Supreme Governor.
Recusant
Catholic refusing to attend Anglican services, fined under Elizabethan legislation.
Northern Rebellion
1569 Catholic uprising by the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland in support of Mary Queen of Scots.
Mary Queen of Scots
Catholic claimant held in English captivity 1568-87; executed at Fotheringhay for the Babington Plot.
Spanish Armada
Fleet of 130 ships sent by Philip II in 1588 to invade England; scattered by English fireships at Calais and storms.
Sea Dogs
Privateers like Drake and Hawkins raiding Spanish shipping with crown approval.
Great Matter
Henry VIII's campaign (1527-33) to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
Act in Restraint of Appeals
1533 statute by Cromwell declaring England an empire and barring appeals to Rome.
Act of Supremacy
1534 Act declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Thomas Cromwell
Chief minister 1532-40 who engineered the Reformation legislation and Dissolution of the Monasteries.
Dissolution of the Monasteries
Suppression of religious houses 1536-40, transferring lands and wealth to the crown.
Pilgrimage of Grace
1536 northern uprising led by Robert Aske protesting religious changes and dissolution.
Battle of Bosworth
Engagement on 22 August 1485 where Henry Tudor defeated Richard III, founding the Tudor dynasty.
Wars of the Roses
Dynastic civil wars (c. 1455-87) between the Houses of Lancaster and York for the English throne.
Bonds and Recognisances
Financial sureties Henry VII used to police noble loyalty by threatening forfeiture for misconduct.
Court of Star Chamber
Royal council acting as a court, used by Henry VII to discipline overmighty subjects.
Pretender
Claimant to the throne; Henry faced Lambert Simnel (1487) and Perkin Warbeck (1491-99).
Treaty of Etaples
1492 agreement with France granting Henry an annual pension and ending support for Warbeck.
Elizabethan Settlement
1559 Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity defining the Church of England with Elizabeth as Supreme Governor.
Royal Injunctions 1559
Orders enforcing the settlement, regulating preaching, vestments and parish discipline.
Thirty-Nine Articles
1563 doctrinal statement giving the Church of England moderate Protestant identity.
Puritanism
Movement seeking further reformation; emerged from Vestiarian Controversy 1565 onwards.
Regnans in Excelsis
Papal bull of 1570 excommunicating Elizabeth and releasing subjects from allegiance.
Jesuit Mission
Catholic missionaries (Campion, Persons) from 1580 seeking to sustain English Catholicism.
Edward VI
Henry VIII's Protestant son (1547-53), under whom England became formally Protestant.
Book of Common Prayer
Cranmer's English liturgy; first edition 1549, more Protestant revision 1552.
Forty-Two Articles
1553 Protestant doctrinal statement that did not become enforced before Edward's death.
Lady Jane Grey
Reluctant Protestant claimant proclaimed queen on 10 July 1553, displaced after nine days by Mary.
Marian Restoration
Mary I's reign (1553-58) reversing Reformation legislation and reuniting England with Rome in 1554.
Marian Persecutions
1555-58 burning of about 280 Protestants including Cranmer (March 1556) for heresy.
Catherine of Aragon
Henry VIII's first wife (married 1509), whose failure to produce a male heir initiated the Great Matter.
Anne Boleyn
Henry's second wife, married January 1533 and crowned in June; executed in May 1536.
Act of Supremacy 1534
Statute declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England in place of the Pope.
Act of Succession
1534 Act vesting the succession in Anne Boleyn's children and requiring oath; refused by More and Fisher.
Ten Articles
1536 doctrinal statement showing moderate Protestant influence, reduced to three sacraments.
Six Articles
1539 statute reasserting conservative doctrine including transubstantiation; nicknamed 'whip with six strings'.
Thirteenth Amendment
Ratified 6 December 1865 abolishing slavery throughout the United States.
Fourteenth Amendment
Ratified 1868 granting citizenship and equal protection of the laws.
Fifteenth Amendment
Ratified 1870 prohibiting denial of the vote on grounds of race or previous servitude.
Black Codes
Southern state laws after 1865 restricting freed people's rights and forcing them into labour contracts.
Ku Klux Klan
White-supremacist terror organisation founded in Tennessee in 1865 to intimidate Black voters.
Plessy v Ferguson
1896 Supreme Court ruling establishing 'separate but equal', legitimising Jim Crow segregation.
Black Power
Slogan popularised by Stokely Carmichael in June 1966 emphasising racial pride and self-determination.
Black Panther Party
Founded by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton in October 1966 in Oakland, combining armed defence with social programmes.
Kerner Commission
1968 report on urban unrest concluding the US was 'moving toward two societies, one black, one white, separate and unequal'.
MLK assassination
Killing of Martin Luther King Jr. on 4 April 1968 in Memphis, triggering nationwide unrest.
Affirmative Action
Policies, particularly from the 1965 Executive Order 11246, requiring federal contractors to hire without discrimination.
Black Lives Matter
Movement founded in 2013 after George Zimmerman's acquittal in the killing of Trayvon Martin.
Brown v Board of Education
Unanimous Supreme Court ruling on 17 May 1954 declaring school segregation unconstitutional.
Little Rock Nine
Nine Black students escorted by federal troops into Central High School in September 1957.
SCLC
Southern Christian Leadership Conference founded in 1957 by MLK to coordinate non-violent protest.
March on Washington
28 August 1963 demonstration of 250,000 where King delivered 'I Have a Dream'.
Civil Rights Act
1964 federal statute outlawing discrimination on grounds of race, sex or national origin in employment and public accommodations.
Voting Rights Act
1965 federal statute banning literacy tests and authorising federal oversight of registration.
Alliance System
Pre-1914 alignments: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia).
July Crisis
Diplomatic breakdown following Franz Ferdinand's assassination on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo.
Schlieffen Plan
German strategy to defeat France via Belgium in six weeks before turning east on Russia.
Trench Warfare
Static front from late 1914 stretching from the Channel to Switzerland, dominated by machine guns and artillery.
Battle of the Somme
Anglo-French offensive 1 July - 18 November 1916; British suffered 57,470 casualties on day one.
Treaty of Versailles
1919 peace imposing on Germany territorial losses, GBP 6.6 billion reparations and Article 231 war guilt.
Blitzkrieg
Combined-arms warfare pairing armour, infantry and tactical aircraft, demonstrated in France May-June 1940.
Operation Barbarossa
German invasion of the USSR launched on 22 June 1941 with 3 million troops along a 1,800-mile front.
Wannsee Conference
Meeting on 20 January 1942 coordinating the Final Solution, the systematic murder of European Jewry.
Stalingrad
Soviet victory in February 1943 capturing the German Sixth Army, marking the eastern front turning point.
D-Day
Allied invasion of Normandy on 6 June 1944 with 156,000 troops landed on five beaches.
Hiroshima
First atomic bomb dropped on 6 August 1945, killing approximately 80,000 immediately; Nagasaki followed on 9 August.
Appeasement
British policy under Chamberlain of accommodating German revisionist demands to preserve peace.
Rhineland Remilitarisation
Hitler's 7 March 1936 reoccupation of the demilitarised Rhineland in breach of Versailles and Locarno.
Anschluss
Union of Germany and Austria on 12 March 1938 following Nazi pressure on Schuschnigg.
Munich Agreement
29 September 1938 conference where Britain, France, Germany and Italy ceded the Sudetenland to Germany.
Nazi-Soviet Pact
Molotov-Ribbentrop non-aggression treaty signed on 23 August 1939, with secret protocols dividing Eastern Europe.
Invasion of Poland
German attack on 1 September 1939, prompting British and French declarations of war on 3 September.
